definition: A pattern of psychological manipulation in which someone repeatedly makes another person doubt their own memory, perceptions, or sanity, often to gain or keep power over them. The defining features are repetition, denial of reality, and the effect of undermining the target's trust in their own judgment.
misuse_examples: He disagreed with me about the movie ending. That's gaslighting.
She lied once about being late. Total gaslighting.
legitimate_examples: Over several months, my partner kept denying conversations we both took part in and insisted I was imagining things, until I stopped trusting my memory.
In psychology class we compared gaslighting with ordinary disagreement.
guidance: A single lie, a disagreement, or two different memories of one event is not gaslighting by itself. People misremember honestly, and two people can see the same event differently. The term fits best when describing a sustained pattern of denying or rewriting reality that leaves someone doubting their own mind. Only the people involved know what happened; this tool cannot judge it.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: This word may be doing overtime.

definition: In everyday speech, a person seen as vain, self-absorbed, or selfish. Clinically, narcissistic personality disorder (NPD) is a diagnosable condition involving a long-standing pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration, and reduced empathy, among other features. Only a qualified professional can make that diagnosis.
misuse_examples: My coworker took the last coffee. What a narcissist.
He posts a lot of selfies, so he's a narcissist.
legitimate_examples: My psychology textbook lists the criteria for narcissistic personality disorder.
A clinician explained the difference between narcissistic traits and the disorder.
guidance: Selfish, vain, or inconsiderate behavior is not the same as narcissistic personality disorder, and traits exist on a spectrum. Casual use of the word is common, but it is a clinical label, and this tool cannot diagnose anyone. Be especially careful about applying it to a specific real person.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: A diagnosis is not a synonym for 'rude'.
source_title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: narcissistic personality disorder

definition: Literally, poisonous or harmful to health. In informal speech about people, relationships, or workplaces, a broad shorthand for something harmful, draining, or unhealthy. It is not a clinical term, and what it covers varies widely between speakers.
misuse_examples: My friend disagreed with me, so she's toxic.
Anyone who doesn't reply right away is toxic.
legitimate_examples: The factory was fined for dumping toxic waste.
The group chat was full of constant put-downs and threats, which made it a toxic environment for me.
guidance: The word is useful but vague. Naming the specific behavior (insults, control, threats, constant put-downs) usually communicates more than the label. Disagreement or incompatibility is not automatically toxicity, and the literal meaning is perfectly valid.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: Name the behavior. 'Toxic' is not a personality test.

definition: Psychologically, an emotional response to a deeply distressing or life-threatening event such as an accident, assault, abuse, or disaster; reactions vary a great deal between people. In medicine, trauma also means physical injury, as in blunt force trauma.
misuse_examples: The wifi dropped during my meeting. I have trauma now.
Waiting in line for ten minutes gave me trauma.
legitimate_examples: Therapy helped me work through trauma from a car accident.
The emergency department treats blunt force trauma.
guidance: Hyperbolic use can blur the difference between ordinary frustration and serious distress, but jokes about a bad day are not an attack on anyone's real experience. This tool does not and cannot decide whether anyone's experience counts as trauma; it only notes when the word sits next to everyday-inconvenience wording.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: Buffering is not a clinical event.

definition: In a mental-health setting, a trigger is something, such as a sound, place, or reminder, that sets off distressing memories or reactions connected to a past experience. Informally, especially online, 'triggered' also just means provoked or annoyed.
misuse_examples: That meme triggered me, lol.
I get so triggered when people chew loudly.
legitimate_examples: The smell of smoke triggered a panic response linked to the fire I survived.
The article had a trigger warning at the top.
guidance: The informal meaning is a normal part of the language and is not inherently incorrect. The clinical meaning is different, and the two are easy to blur. This tool does not label informal use as misuse; it only flags that the word has two meanings, and context is what separates them.
humor: Two meanings, one word. Context does the heavy lifting.

definition: A warning sign that something may be wrong. In talk about relationships and workplaces, it usually means a behavior or fact that suggests a possible problem, and how serious it is depends entirely on context.
misuse_examples: He likes a different sports team than I do. Red flag.
She takes a long time to answer texts. Huge red flag.
legitimate_examples: He kept pressuring me to cut off my friends, which was a real red flag.
The contract had several red flags that our lawyer pointed out.
guidance: 'Red flag' is a broad, informal phrase, and humorous use is common and fine. It works best when the warning sign is specific, such as controlling behavior, threats, or dishonesty about something important. One quirk or difference is usually not a pattern.
humor: Not every difference is a flag. Some are just Tuesday.

definition: A pattern of overwhelming affection, attention, or gifts, often very early in a relationship, that may be used to build influence or control over someone. Intent and pattern matter: the term is about excess used as a tool, not about warmth itself.
misuse_examples: He texted me good morning, so that's love bombing.
She said she liked me on the second date. Love bombing.
legitimate_examples: He showered me with gifts and constant attention, then became cold and controlling when I wanted time with friends.
We discussed the idea of love bombing in a workshop on healthy relationships.
guidance: Enthusiastic affection is not automatically love bombing, and some people simply move fast or express feelings openly. The concern is a pattern: intensity that pressures, isolates, or is followed by withdrawal or control. This is a popular term, not a formal clinical diagnosis, and this tool cannot judge anyone's intent.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: A compliment is not a bomb.

definition: Describes influencing someone through indirect, deceptive, or exploitative tactics, typically for one's own benefit and at the other person's expense. It is distinct from ordinary persuasion, from openly asking for something, and from disagreeing.
misuse_examples: She asked me to help her move. So manipulative.
He convinced me to try sushi. Manipulative.
legitimate_examples: He lied about money and used guilt-trips to pressure me into signing.
The marketing course covered manipulative sales tactics and how to spot them.
guidance: Asking for a favor, making an honest argument, or saying no is not manipulation. Manipulation typically involves deception, pressure, or exploiting someone's vulnerabilities. People are often unaware of what they are doing, so the label says little about intent, and this tool cannot assess it.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: Asking nicely is not a heist.

definition: In relationships, personal limits about what a person will accept, do, or engage in, and what they will do if a limit is crossed. A boundary describes your own choices and actions, such as 'I will leave the room if I am shouted at'. The word also has plain geographic and legal meanings.
misuse_examples: My boundary is that you can't talk to your friends anymore.
Boundaries mean you have to do what I say.
legitimate_examples: I told her I won't lend money, and that I'd end the call if the shouting continued.
The survey marked the property boundaries.
guidance: A boundary governs what you do, not what another adult is allowed to do. Requests and preferences are fine, but demands that control someone else's friendships, movements, or choices are better described as rules or ultimatums. Healthy limits and honest disagreement can coexist; context matters.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: A boundary is a fence for you, not a leash for them.

definition: A response style that insists on staying positive and dismisses or minimizes difficult emotions, for example telling someone who is grieving to just look on the bright side. The term describes the dismissal of feelings, not optimism or kindness itself.
misuse_examples: My friend was happy for me when I got the job. Toxic positivity.
Anyone who is optimistic is toxic positivity.
legitimate_examples: When I said I was grieving, he just said 'good vibes only' and changed the subject.
We discussed how toxic positivity can shut down honest conversation.
guidance: Being cheerful, hopeful, or encouraging is not toxic positivity. The issue arises when positivity is used to shut down or dismiss real difficulty. Intent is often kind, which is why context matters. This is a popular term, not a clinical one.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: Cheerfulness is allowed to exist.

definition: Mostly an internet catchphrase used humorously to react to a burn or a mildly painful remark. Outside the meme, emotional harm is a real concept: lasting distress caused by experiences such as ongoing abuse or mistreatment.
misuse_examples: He took the last fries. That's emotional damage.
My team lost. Emotional damage, lol.
legitimate_examples: Years of verbal abuse caused her real emotional harm, and she is working through it in therapy.
Someone shouted 'emotional damage' after the joke, and everyone laughed.
guidance: Used as a joke, the phrase is simply slang and is not incorrect. It is not a clinical term or a diagnosis. The serious sense relates to sustained harm and is separate from the meme. Context decides which one is meant.
humor: Slang is allowed. So is sincerity. Context sorts them out.

definition: Not a single diagnosis. Attachment theory studies how early bonds with caregivers shape later relationships and describes styles such as secure, anxious, avoidant, and disorganized. Reactive attachment disorder is a specific diagnosis in children linked to severe neglect, and a professional must make it.
misuse_examples: He texts me a lot, so he has attachment issues.
She's clingy, which means attachment issues.
legitimate_examples: My therapist explained how my anxious attachment style developed from my early childhood.
The seminar covered attachment theory and reactive attachment disorder.
guidance: Liking closeness, texting often, or being sad after a breakup is not evidence of attachment issues. Attachment styles are research concepts describing tendencies, not defects, and they can shift over time. Labeling a real person from a few behaviors is unreliable, and this tool cannot assess anyone.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: Texting back is not a syndrome.
source_title: APA Dictionary of Psychology: attachment theory

definition: The verb form of gaslighting: to repeatedly manipulate someone into doubting their own memory, perceptions, or sanity. As with the noun, it describes a pattern of sustained manipulation, not a single lie or a disagreement.
misuse_examples: He disagreed with me, so he's trying to gaslight me.
She forgot our plan, and now she's gaslighting me.
legitimate_examples: He would gaslight me by denying things he said, until I second-guessed my memory over time.
The article explains what it means to gaslight someone and how to recognize it.
guidance: Wrong, mistaken, or forgetful is not gaslighting. Gaslighting involves repeated denial or distortion of reality that erodes someone's trust in their own mind. Context matters, and this tool cannot judge anyone's actions or intent.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: Being wrong is not a power move.

definition: A popular term for emotional or psychological abuse attributed to a person with narcissistic traits. It is not a formal clinical diagnosis, and how it is defined varies between writers and communities.
misuse_examples: He argued with me about dinner. Narcissistic abuse.
She was rude once. That's narcissistic abuse.
legitimate_examples: She described years of manipulation and put-downs in her relationship, and later joined a support group for survivors.
The article discussed narcissistic abuse and why the term is debated.
guidance: Abuse can be real and serious whether or not the other person has any particular personality traits, and you do not need a label for the other person to recognize harm. The term is contested, since it is a popular rather than a clinical category. A single rude moment or argument is not abuse. This tool cannot judge any real situation.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: An argument over dinner is not an abuse category.

definition: A popular term for unloading heavy, distressing experiences onto someone without checking whether they have the capacity, consent, or context to receive them, such as sharing graphic details with a stranger or a coworker who did not ask. It is not a clinical term, and its use is debated.
misuse_examples: My friend told me she had a bad week. Trauma dumping.
Any time someone vents, it's trauma dumping.
legitimate_examples: A new acquaintance unloaded years of painful details on me within minutes and never asked whether I had the energy to listen.
We talked about how to check in before sharing something heavy.
guidance: Sharing difficult feelings with someone who is willing to listen is normal and healthy, and so is seeking support. The concern is about consent, capacity, and setting rather than about the content of what someone feels. Nobody should be shamed for needing to talk, and this tool cannot judge anyone's disclosure.
humor: POSSIBLE MISUSE: A bad day is allowed to be mentioned.
